messages.author: 27a41bc7af493a55
messages.subject: lp_ correlated with parameter
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to fit the hierarchical model pasted below to a pretty large dataset (60 subjects and 30000 variables per subject). For lp_ and log_slope_sigmac_sigma, Rhat is a bit over 1.1 - see the traceplot. Also, these two parameters seem very correlated - see the scatterplot. Any suggestion how to get them to converge?

I'm using half gaussians for the priors for the 4 hyperparameters representing standard deviations (those ending in _sigma). Is this a problem or should I go for another distribution? I tried with half cauchy but the sampling was too slow, and it is already taking me a week to fit this model, given the large number of parameters.

I would appreciate any comments.
Best, Benjamin 

--------------------------------


data {
   int<lower=0> S;          // number of subjects
   int<lower=0> C;          // number of values per subject
   vector[C] values[S]; // values
   vector[S] age; // age
}

parameters {

   real<lower=-1, upper=1> intercept_muc_mu;
   real<lower=0> intercept_muc_sigma;
   real<lower=-.01, upper=.01> slope_muc_mu;
   real<lower=0> slope_muc_sigma;

   real<lower=-4, upper=0> log_intercept_sigmac_mu;
   real<lower=0> log_intercept_sigmac_sigma;
   real<lower=-.03, upper=.03> log_slope_sigmac_mu;
   real<lower=0> log_slope_sigmac_sigma;

   vector<lower=-2, upper=2>[C] intercept_muc;
   vector<lower=-.03, upper=.03>[C] slope_muc;
   vector<lower=-6, upper=1>[C] log_intercept_sigmac;
   vector<lower=-.03, upper=.03>[C] log_slope_sigmac;

}

transformed parameters {

     vector[C] muc[S];
     vector[C] sigmac[S];
    
     for (s in 1:S){
       muc[s] <- intercept_muc + slope_muc*age[s];
       sigmac[s] <- exp(log_intercept_sigmac + log_slope_sigmac*age[s]);
     }


}


model {

   // priors
   intercept_muc_mu ~ normal(0, .5);
   intercept_muc_sigma ~ normal(0, .1);
   slope_muc_mu ~ normal(0, .005);
   slope_muc_sigma ~ normal(0, .01);

   log_intercept_sigmac_mu ~ uniform(-4, 0);
   log_intercept_sigmac_sigma ~ normal(0, .1); 
   log_slope_sigmac_mu ~ normal(0, .01);
   log_slope_sigmac_sigma ~ normal(0, .05);

   intercept_muc ~ normal(intercept_muc_mu, intercept_muc_sigma);
   slope_muc ~ normal(slope_muc_mu, slope_muc_sigma);
   log_intercept_sigmac ~ normal(log_intercept_sigmac_mu, log_intercept_sigmac_sigma);
   log_slope_sigmac ~ normal(log_slope_sigmac_mu, log_slope_sigmac_sigma);

     for (s in 1:S)
    values[s] ~ normal(muc[s], sigmac[s]);

}

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: lp_ correlated with parameter
parts:
On Friday, September 23, 2016 at 11:02:53 AM UTC-4, Benjamin Garzon wrote:
I'm trying to fit the hierarchical model pasted below to a pretty large dataset (60 subjects and 30000 variables per subject). For lp_ and log_slope_sigmac_sigma, Rhat is a bit over 1.1 - see the traceplot. Also, these two parameters seem very correlated - see the scatterplot.

Correlation between unknowns is not, by itself, a problem. In particular, the correlation between a parameter and lp__ is definitely not a problem. It would be a problem if the log posterior kernel were completely independent from that parameter because then that parameter would be unidentified. Basically, a pairs plot is not for visualizing the existence of posterior correlations, it is for diagnosing when there are sampling problems. (I would guess that there are a bunch of divergent transition and / or maximum treedepth warnings with your model that you didn't mention). The pairs() function in rstan is designed for this purpose, whereas a hand-rolled pairs plot presumably is not.

Nor is it a problem if a parameter is correlated with a transformed parameter or a generated quantity because the dependence is built in by the transformation. Correlation between primitive parameters (particularly when it is non-constant) combined with different scales and / or funnel effects can make it more difficult for Stan to sample efficiently.

I'm using half gaussians for the priors for the 4 hyperparameters representing standard deviations (those ending in _sigma). Is this a problem or should I go for another distribution? I tried with half cauchy but the sampling was too slow, and it is already taking me a week to fit this model, given the large number of parameters.

Which distribution represents your prior beliefs? FWIW, a half-Cauchy often yields poor performance so we are not recommending it as much any more, but if your beliefs are half-Cauchy then go with it no matter how long it takes to run. That being said, some of the reason why it takes so long are self-inflicted. This line
for (s in 1:S) values[s] ~ normal(muc[s], sigmac[s]);

should be

values ~ normal(muc, sigmac);

to prevent a lot of unnecessary memory allocations. This line

log_intercept_sigmac_mu ~ uniform(-4, 0);

can be omitted because all it does it check whether log_intercept_sigmac_mu is between -4 and 0, which is true by construction. That said, two-sided bounds on parameters do not perform well if the posterior mass piles up on the boundaries. Worse, using normal priors for a parameter that is bounded on both sides when either the mean or the standard deviation or both is unknown yields the wrong answer because your prior does not integrate to a constant over the interval of support for that parameter. You have to either truncate the prior or more plausibly, eliminate the bounds on the parameter's support.

It is often but not always better in hierarchical models to use non-centered parameterizations that take advantage of the fact that the normal distribution is in the scale-location family so rather than having something like

target += normal_lpdf(x | a, b);

where x, a, and b are unknown you can do something like

target += normal_lpdf(z | 0, 1);

in the model block and do

x = a + b * z;

in the transformed parameters block. This transformation, which is also known as the Matt Trick, is discussed in the manual and many times on stan-users.

Ben

parts:
You're right that you can't vectorize the value[s] ~ ...
statement any more than you have.

I'd suggest priors rather than hard constraints.
And if you still get these problems, lower the stepsize
and increase adapt_delta, which should force the stepsize
lower and help avoid boundaries.

But the bigger problem is that you're mixing scales with:

> real<lower=-.03, upper=.03> log_slope_sigmac_mu;

It helps if all the parameters are on the unit scale (that is,
have roughly 1 standard deviation in the posterior). You can
either rescale predictors so this happens, or change the variables
to be something like:

real log_slope_sigmac_mu_raw;

real log_slope_sigmac_mu;
log_slope_sigmac_mu = 0.03 * real log_slope_sigmac_mu_raw;

log_slope_sigmac_mu_raw ~ normal(0, 1);

- Bob

messages.author: 49e107cb0f8a3d27
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] lp_ correlated with parameter (ADVI convergence)
parts:
as bob notes, the error output is a result of the parameterization. ADVI uses stochastic gradients to optimize its objective and will drop samples that produce infinite values; such infinite values can occur when taking the exp of very large values. usually this is not a problem.

one suggestion is to set the argument which increases the maximum number of dropped gradients.

another suggestion is to use the softplus transformation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks)). i’ve found this to be more stable than exp transformations in practice. (to manually define the transformation, you need to perform the transformation in the transformed parameters block, and then manually add the log det to your model block.)

dustin

The parens cause problems for me clicking through, but the
page is there:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rectifier_(neural_networks)

The rectifier is

f(x) = max(0, x)

which looks an awful lot like "hinge loss" from SVMs; the
"soft" version the Wikipedia suggests is:

f(x) = log(1 + exp(x))

Stan has a builtin for this:

log1p_exp(x) = log(1 + exp(x)).

And the derivative is also built-in:

log1p_exp'(x) = 1/(1 + exp(x)) * exp(x) = inv_logit(x)

So the log Jacobian is also a built-in:

log_inv_logit(x)

I think I did that right.

- Bob

Yup, it is the hinge loss used in SVMs.

In general I like softplus because its gradient doesn’t increase as quickly as exp. More details and discussion of transformations are also here: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-dev/6iP0DzW5Yec
(a numerically stable way of implementing softplus is also written there)

Dustin
